verses.1:1: And the word of the Lord came to Jonah the son of Amittai, saying,
verses.1:2: "Rise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and proclaim in it, for the outcry of its evil has come up to Me."
verses.1:3: And Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish, and paid the fare for it and went aboard it to sail with them to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord.
verses.1:4: And the Lord stirred up a wind upon the sea, and a great tempest arose in the sea, and the ship was in danger of being shattered.
verses.1:5: And the sailors were afraid and cried out, each one to his god, and they jettisoned the goods that were in the ship into the sea, so as to be lightened of them; but Jonah had gone down into the hold of the ship, and was sleeping and snoring.
verses.1:6: And the first mate came to him and said to him, "Why are you snoring? Rise and call upon your god, so that God may rescue us and we may not perish."
verses.1:7: And each one said to his companion, "Come, let us cast lots and find out on whose account this evil is among us." And they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah.
verses.1:8: And they said to him, "Tell us, what is your occupation, and where do you come from, and from what country and from what people are you?"
verses.1:9: And he said to them, "I am a servant of the Lord, and I revere the Lord God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land."
verses.1:10: And the men feared with a great fear and said to him, "What is this you have done?" For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the Lord, because he had told them.
verses.1:11: And they said to him, "What shall we do to you so that the sea will subside from us?" For the sea kept advancing and stirring up a tempest all the more.
verses.1:12: And Jonah said to them, "Lift me up and cast me into the sea, and the sea will subside from you; for I know that because of me this great tempest is upon you."
verses.1:13: And the men strove hard to turn back to the land, and they were not able, because the sea kept advancing and was being stirred up all the more against them.
verses.1:14: And they cried out to the Lord and said, "By no means, Lord! Let us not perish on account of this man's life, and do not lay righteous blood upon us, for You, Lord, have done just as You desired."
verses.1:15: And they took Jonah and cast him out into the sea, and the sea ceased from its tossing.
verses.1:16: And the men feared the Lord with great fear, and they offered sacrifices to the Lord and vowed vows.
verses.2:1: And the Lord commanded a great sea monster to swallow Jonah; and Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster three days and three nights.
verses.2:2: And Jonah prayed to the Lord his God out of the belly of the sea monster,
verses.2:3: and said, "I cried out in my distress to the Lord my God, and He listened to me. Out of the belly of Hades You heard my cry, my voice; You hurled me into the depths of the heart of the sea,
verses.2:4: and rivers surrounded me; all Your swells and Your waves passed over me.
verses.2:5: And I said, 'I have been driven away from Your eyes; shall I indeed look again toward Your holy temple?'
verses.2:6: Water poured around me even to the soul, the uttermost abyss surrounded me, my head sank into the clefts of the mountains;
verses.2:7: I went down into a land whose bars are everlasting barriers; and let the corruption of my life come up, Lord my God.
verses.2:8: When my soul was failing from me, I remembered the Lord, and may my prayer come to You, into Your holy temple.
verses.2:9: Those who observe empty and false things have forsaken their mercy.
verses.2:10: But I, with a voice of praise and thanksgiving, will sacrifice to You; all that I have vowed I will pay to You, for deliverance to the Lord."
verses.2:11: And the sea monster was commanded, and it cast Jonah out onto the dry land.
verses.3:1: And the word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, saying,
verses.3:2: "Rise, go to Nineveh, the great city, and proclaim in it according to the former proclamation that I spoke to you."
verses.3:3: And Jonah rose and went to Nineveh, just as the Lord had spoken. Now Nineveh was a great city to God, about a journey of three days' walk.
verses.3:4: And Jonah began to enter into the city about one day's journey, and he proclaimed and said, "Three more days, and Nineveh will be overthrown."
verses.3:5: And the men of Nineveh believed God, and they proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them to the least of them.
verses.3:6: And the word reached the king of Nineveh; and he rose up from his throne, and took off his robe from himself and wrapped himself in sackcloth, and sat on ashes.
verses.3:7: And it was proclaimed and spoken in Nineveh from the king and from his nobles, saying, "Let the people and the livestock and the cattle and the sheep taste nothing, nor graze, nor drink water."
verses.3:8: And the people and the livestock wrapped themselves in sackcloth, and they cried out to God earnestly; and each one turned away from his wicked way and from the injustice that was in their hands, saying,
verses.3:9: "Who knows if God will relent and turn away from the anger of His wrath, and we will by no means perish?"
verses.3:10: And God saw their deeds, that they turned away from their wicked ways; and God relented concerning the evil that He had spoken to do to them, and He did not do it.
verses.4:1: And Jonah was grieved with great grief, and he was agitated.
verses.4:2: And he prayed to the Lord and said, "Oh, Lord, were not these my words while I was still in my land? For this reason I acted beforehand to flee to Tarshish, because I knew that You are merciful and compassionate, slow to anger and abundant in mercy, and relenting over calamities.
verses.4:3: And now, Sovereign Lord, take my life from me, because it is better for me to die than for me to live."
verses.4:4: And the Lord said to Jonah, "Are you deeply grieved?"
verses.4:5: And Jonah went out from the city and sat down opposite the city; and he made a shelter for himself there and was sitting underneath it in the shade, until he could see what would become of the city.
verses.4:6: And the Lord God commanded a gourd, and it came up over Jonah's head to be shade above his head, to shade him from his troubles; and Jonah rejoiced over the gourd with great joy.
verses.4:7: And God commanded a worm at dawn on the next day, and it struck the gourd, and it withered away.
verses.4:8: And it happened, as soon as the sun rose, that God commanded a burning wind of scorching heat, and the sun struck upon Jonah's head; and he grew faint and despaired of his life, and said, "Better for me to die than to live."
verses.4:9: And God said to Jonah, "Are you deeply grieved over the gourd?" And he said, "I am deeply grieved, to the point of death."
verses.4:10: And the Lord said, "You had pity on the gourd, for which you did not toil and which you did not nurture, which came into being overnight and overnight perished.
verses.4:11: And shall I not have pity on Nineveh, the great city, in which more than 120,000 people dwell, who do not know their right hand or their left hand, and many animals?"

notes.1:2: The Greek reads "in it" (ἐν αὐτῇ) rather than "against it," and includes "the outcry" (ἡ κραυγή) before "of its evil," reflecting distinctive Septuagint wording compared to the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.1:6: Greek πρωρεύς denotes the prow officer or first mate (second in command of a vessel), and ῥέγχεις ("snoring," as in 1:5) specifically depicts Jonah's heavy sleep as snoring.
notes.1:9: The Greek reads "a servant of the Lord" (Δοῦλος Κυρίου) rather than "a Hebrew" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, reflecting a different reading of the underlying Hebrew consonants.
notes.1:14: Greek Μηδαμῶς ("By no means") renders a Hebrew particle of entreaty as a strong negation, and αἷμα δίκαιον specifies "righteous blood" rather than "innocent blood."
notes.2:1: Greek κῆτος denotes a huge sea creature or sea monster rather than an ordinary fish; in the Septuagint versification, this verse opens chapter 2 (corresponding to 1:17 in most English Bibles).
notes.2:3: The Greek places both "my cry" (κραυγῆς μου) and "my voice" (φωνῆς μου) in the genitive as objects of "You heard," and renders Sheol as Hades (ᾅδης).
notes.2:6: The Septuagint reads "uttermost abyss" (ἄβυσσος ... ἐσχάτη, reading the Hebrew word for "reeds" as "end/uttermost") and "my head sank into the clefts of the mountains" rather than seaweed wrapping around Jonah's head.
notes.2:7: The Greek text has a third-person imperative with "corruption" as subject (ἀναβήτω φθορὰ ζωῆς μου, "let the corruption of my life come up") rather than "You brought up my life from the pit" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.2:10: The closing phrase σωτηρίου τῷ κυρίῳ uses the genitive ("for deliverance to the Lord") rather than the independent clause "salvation belongs to the Lord" found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.3:2: The Greek specifies "according to the former proclamation that I spoke to you" in the past tense, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to the proclamation God is about to tell Jonah.
notes.3:3: "A great city to God" (πόλις μεγάλη τῷ θεῷ) preserves the literal Semitic idiom expressing extraordinary size ("great even in God's sight").
notes.3:4: The Septuagint reads "three days" (τρεῖς ἡμέραι) rather than "forty days" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.3:8: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text, where the king's decree continues through this verse, the Greek shifts to past-tense indicative verbs describing the Ninevites' repentance and ends with plural "saying" (λέγοντες), attributing verse 9 to the people.
notes.4:1: The Greek describes Jonah's reaction as intense grief and agitation rather than anger, establishing the motif of grief that continues in verses 4 and 9.
notes.4:4: The Greek asks whether Jonah is deeply or exceedingly grieved, taking the underlying Hebrew idiom adverbially rather than asking whether it is right for him to be angry.
notes.4:6: The Greek identifies the plant specifically as a gourd (kolokynthe) and reads "to shade him" rather than "to deliver him" as in the Hebrew text.
notes.4:8: The Greek reads "a burning wind of scorching heat" without specifying an east wind, and says Jonah "despaired of his life" (renounced or gave up on his life) rather than asking to die.
notes.4:10: The Greek verb pheidomai ("spare") with hyper carries the Septuagintal sense "have pity on," connecting Jonah's pity for the gourd with God's sparing of Nineveh in verse 11.
